extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining loss-of-right/prior-art issues under 35 U.S.C. 102 (public use, on-sale, experimental use, abandonment, foreign priority, and 102(e) references) during patent examination and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors indicative of an experimental purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have considered a number of factors in determining whether a claimed invention was the subject of a commercial offer for sale primarily for purposes of experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors include: (1) necessity for public testing; (2) amount of control over the experiment retained by the inventor; (3) nature of the invention; (4) length of the test period; (5) whether payment was made; (6) whether there was a secrecy obligation; (7) whether records of the experiment were kept; (8) who conducted the experiment; (9) degree of commercial exploitation during testing; (10) whether the invention reasonably requires evaluation under actual conditions of use; (11) whether testing was systematically performed; (12) whether the inventor continually monitored the invention during testing; and (13) nature of contacts made with potential customers. Case law: Allen Eng’g Corp. v. Bartell Indus., Inc., quoting EZ Dock v. Schafer Sys., Inc.; Electromotive Div. of GM v. Transportation Sys. Div. of GE (customer awareness critical). No single factor or combination is necessarily determinative; examiner must assess scope and length of activity relative to experimental purpose and subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control and customer awareness required for experimental use
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant determinative factors are the extent of supervision and control maintained by an inventor during alleged experimentation and the customer's awareness of the purported testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inventor relinquishes supervision/control and places the invention into unrestricted use, a 35 U.S.C. 102(b) bar results. Customer must be made aware of experimentation where sales occur in ordinary commercial environments; secretly held subjective intent to experiment is insufficient without objective evidence (LaBounty; Paragon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use ends upon actual reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental use means perfecting/completing an invention to the point of determining that it will work for its intended purpose; experimental use ends with an actual reduction to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If examiner concludes applicant considered invention 'complete,' awaiting approvals (e.g., Underwriters' Laboratories) will not normally overcome this. Lack of modifications resulting from alleged experimentation is evidence (though not conclusive) that activity was not experimental. Modifications/refinements that did result must be features of the claimed invention to have probative value. Cases: RCA Corp. v. Data Gen.; InterRoyal; Skil Corp.; In re Theis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of the invention as a bar to experimental exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor considered the invention to be 'complete' prior to activity alleged as experimental, that activity will not normally be considered experimental use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should evaluate whether evidence shows the inventor was satisfied invention was complete. Evidence that alleged experimental activity did not lead to specific modifications supports that the activity was commercial rather than experimental. Any modifications arising from experimentation must be part of the claimed invention to be probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposal of prototypes before critical date
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prototype has been disposed of by an inventor before the critical date, inquiry should focus on inventor intent and reasonableness of the disposal under all circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidental income from reasonable disposal is not necessarily fatal (In re Dybel). However, if prototype was 'complete' and experimentation ceased, unrestricted disposal constitutes a 35 U.S.C. 102(b) bar (In re Blaisdell). Cases may conflict (Watson v. Allen). Examiner should assess intent and restraints on subsequent use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted experimental activity and testing (developmental testing permitted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Testing of an invention in the normal context of technological development and experimentation to determine utility may be permissible under 35 U.S.C. 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: testing chemical compositions with no known utility to find utility is likely permissible absent sales/commercial exploitation (General Motors v. Bendix). However, testing solely to determine product acceptance (market testing) is not permitted. 'Minor tune up' procedures that do not require inventor skill may not fall within the exception (In re Theis). Examiner to distinguish permissible developmental testing from activities that amount to commercial exploitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental activity in design applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Public use of an ornamental design to generate consumer interest is not an experimental use, but experimentation targeting functional features of a product containing an ornamental design may negate what would otherwise be public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display of a design at trade show can be public use (In re Mann). But studies evaluating functional features (e.g., student evaluations of a spice container's functional aspects) may be experimental and negate public use (Tone Brothers v. Sysco). Examiner must distinguish ornament-focused displays from functional testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use exception is personal to the applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory experimental-use exception is personal to an applicant; public use or on-sale activity by another party is generally effective against the applicant unless the activity was under the applicant's supervision and control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of experimental activity by another party will not overcome a prima facie 102(b) case unless the activity was supervised/controlled by the applicant (Magnetics v. Arnold Eng’g; Bourne v. Jones). Examiner to require proof of applicant's supervision/control when third-party activity is asserted as experimental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market testing is not permitted as experimental use
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimentation to determine product acceptance (market testing) is typical of a trader's experiment and is not within the experimental-use exception under 35 U.S.C. 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market testing indicates commercial exploitation rather than inventor experimentation and will not avoid statutory bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment under 35 U.S.C. 102(c) must be intentional
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual abandonment requires the inventor intend to abandon the invention; intent may be implied from conduct but should not be imputed lightly; reasonable doubt resolved in favor of the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay alone is insufficient to infer abandonment (Moore v. United States). Evidence such as deliberate surrender/dedication to public, or conduct indicating active promotion by others while inventor does nothing, can support abandonment (Davis Harvester). Ex parte Dunne; In re Gibbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay in reapplying after abandonment of prior application
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay in reapplying for patent after abandonment of a previous application does not constitute abandonment under 35 U.S.C. 102(c) absent evidence of expressed intent or conduct to abandon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no evidence of intent to abandon, delay alone insufficient (Petersen v. Fee Int’l). Examiner should look for conduct indicating dedication to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure without claiming in prior issued patent is rebuttable
rubrics_metrics.description: Inference of abandonment from disclosure in a prior issued patent (where subject matter was disclosed but not claimed) is rebuttable by filing an application at any time before a statutory bar arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(c) solely based on issuance of a patent that disclosed (but did not claim) the subject matter is improper if applicant timely files; see In re Gibbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lapse of time bars only in priority contests (102(g)/102(c) context)
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere lapse of time will not bar a patent except where there is a priority contest and the applicant abandons, suppresses, or conceals the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandonment, suppression, and concealment are treated under 35 U.S.C. 102(g); see MPEP § 2138.03 for details (Panduit Corp. v. Dennison Mfg. Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(d) — four requirements for foreign-prior barred
rubrics_metrics.description: To bar a U.S. patent under 102(d), four conditions must be present: (A) foreign application filed more than 12 months before effective U.S. filing date; (B) foreign application filed by same applicant or legal representative/assigns; (C) foreign patent or inventor's certificate actually granted before U.S. filing date; (D) same invention is involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner to verify each of the four requirements. See MPEP § 2135.01 for clarification and case examples. A continuation-in-part may break priority chain relative to foreign parents; anniversary date falling on weekend/holiday extends to next business day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'patented' and treatment of foreign published/allowed applications under 102(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Patented' means a formal bestowal of patent rights (grant/sealing). A published application is not a 'patent' for 102(d), but an allowed application published for opposition may be treated as a 'patent' for 102(d) purposes if substantial provisional enforcement rights arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical date is when foreign patent becomes enforceable (issue/seal/grant). Periods of secrecy after grant do not alter 102(d) applicability. Cases: In re Monks; Ex parte Beik; In re Kathawala; Gramme Elec. Co. Older foreign forms (e.g., Gebrauchsmuster) may be treated as patents if they grant exclusionary rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revised 35 U.S.C. 102(e) post-AIPA/IPHTTA (prior art dates and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revised 35 U.S.C. 102(e) (AIPA 1999 and technical amendments 2002) applies retroactively and allows the use of certain international application publications and U.S. patent/application publications as prior art as of their respective U.S. filing dates (including certain international filing dates), with limited exceptions for international applications filed prior to Nov 29, 2000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The revised provisions supersede previous versions of 102(e)/374 except for certain international applications filed before Nov 29, 2000. The prior-art date of a reference under 102(e) may be the international filing date if requirements (designation of the U.S., WIPO publication in English under PCT Art.21(2)) are met. See MPEP § 706.02(f)(1) for application guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Invention Registrations (SIRs) are prior art under 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: A published SIR is treated the same as a U.S. patent for defensive purposes and is usable as a reference as of its filing date under 35 U.S.C. 102, including 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per 35 U.S.C. 157(c) and MPEP § 1111, SIRs are prior art under the same rules as U.S. patents for 102(e) rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defensive publications are prior art only as of publication date (not filing date)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defensive Publication Program outputs are publications, not patents or application publications under 35 U.S.C. 122(b); therefore they are prior art only as of their publication date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defensive publications cannot be relied on as of their filing date for 102(e) purposes (Ex parte Osmond). See MPEP § 711.06(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: When a U.S. application becomes available as prior art under 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is no common assignee or inventor, a U.S. application must issue as a patent or be published as a SIR or as an application publication before it is available as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain U.S. application publications and international application publications with earlier effective U.S. filing dates can be prior art; see MPEP § 706.02(a) for specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional 102(e) rejection when common assignee or inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is a common assignee or inventor, an examiner may provisionally reject a later application over an earlier filed, unpublished, copending U.S. application under 35 U.S.C. 102(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: put applicant on notice early and allow fullest opportunity to overcome rejection by amendment or evidence. Provisional rejections are authorized only when there is a common inventor or assignee; otherwise the earlier-filed copending application remains confidential. See Ex parte Irish; Ex parte Bartfeld. Note limitations: for applications filed on/after Nov 29, 1999 or pending on/after Dec 10, 2004, a provisional 103(a) rejection using 102(e) prior art is not proper if evidence shows common ownership/assignment at time invention made. CREATE Act and 103(c) issues further affect disqualification of certain references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content of prior art available under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection may rely on any part of the patent or application publication disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The entire disclosure of a U.S. patent, U.S. patent application publication, or qualifying international application publication can be relied upon to reject claims; see Sun Studs, Inc. v. ATA Equip. Leasing, Inc. (Fed. Cir.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference must itself contain the subject matter relied upon
rubrics_metrics.description: When using a U.S. patent, application publication, or international application publication under 102(e), the disclosure relied on must be present in the issued patent or application publication itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject matter canceled from the application, or present only in a parent but not in the child CIP publication/issued patent, cannot be relied upon as of the child's filing/publication date (Ex parte Stalego; In re Lund). Examiner must verify that the specific subject matter relied upon actually appears in the reference document being relied on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court authorization of 103 rejections based on 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has authorized the use of 102(e) references as bases for 35 U.S.C. 103 obviousness rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner may rely on 102(e) references when determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103, subject to other statutory and policy limitations (see MPEP discussion and case law).
